title: Gateless Barrier, Case 16: Yun-men: The Sound of the Bell
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up case 16 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Yunmen asks why a monk puts on the seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell when the world is vast and wide. Nomon sorts it as a one-sentence teaching phrase, recalls Katagiri Roshi's "Great autumn moon, high in sky" at a City Center sesshin, and traces the robe to the Buddha's rice-field story. Koun Yamada's comment on the "why" and Wumen's question of whether sound comes to the ear or the ear goes to the sound lead to Wumen's verse, whose second couplet reverses the first. Nomon closes by sparing the sixty blows.

sentences.text: Lately we added a little element.
There's a particular way that the jisha is supposed to give you the lector, and before we just plonked it down and moved it over.
It's even more servant-like, but it's good to learn the ways that it's done.
So anyway, here we are again.
The gang's all here, it looks like.
With these three stories, number 14, 15, and today 16, in the Mumonkan, we actually get to meet three of the main types of stories that they have in these collections.
First, Monday.
Does that seem a while ago?
Monday we had a dramatic play, a theatrical production.

Multiple people involved, the monks of the East Hall and the West Hall, and the teacher majestically swooping in and grabbing the cat, and the other student, Zhaozhou, arriving later, putting his sandal on his head in shame.
And dramatic dialogue, right?
"Who can say a word of Zen?
If you were here, you would have saved the cat."
So we had a dramatic play, case 14.
Case 15, we had a long dialogue, really just two characters, student and teacher, monk and master.
"Where are you from?"
"Ah, I spare you 60 blows."
And both of those two forms were actually two-parters, did you notice that?
Sometimes there's more than two parts, but usually at least two.
First the altercation around the cat, and then the wise student returns.
First the initial dialogue, and then poor Dongshan had his tough night, lost in an ocean of yes and no thinking, and then meeting the teacher again the next morning, part two.
So today we have the third major type of koan, which is very simple: a teaching phrase, a saying of the teacher.
These are usually offered quite unadorned, one sentence, the whole story is one sentence.
I think in Western literature we wouldn't be satisfied with one-sentence stories.
But here we can endlessly comment on them.
If it's a poem, it's okay if it's one sentence, I think.
Remember once Norman wrote a whole collection of one-sentence poems?
I forget which book that's in.
I didn't really like them very much.
So here's the entire case 16 of the Mumonkan.
*Yun Men said, the world is vast and wide.
Why do you put on your seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell?
Yun Men said the world is vast and wide.
Why do you put on your seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell?*
This is the same teacher as in the previous case, the same Yun Men.
Eighth century, I think.
And that's the whole story.
We can make up a context for this story, and it's traditional actually.
So we can picture it and enter into the story, which is another big part of this literature.
The idea is not to read it at arm's length like literature, but to enter into it in some way.
What would you say?
A few people were thinking about that and came and told me what they were thinking.
If the teacher ferociously asked you, "Where are you from?" what would you do?
How would you hear these words of Yun Men?
"The world is vast and wide.
Why do you put on your robe at the sound of the bell?"
Maybe these are words given in the zendo during zazen, maybe during evening zazen.
That's a traditional thing to do: a few words spoken into the silence.
I thought about offering some words like that, encouraging words, last night, but it was so quiet in here I didn't want to interrupt you.
So peaceful.

But it can be really helpful to receive those words, whether you're settled or your mind is going a million miles an hour, to receive some words from outside this little ecosystem that we get lost in.
I keep remembering things from long ago lately, but I was remembering the one sesshin I sat with Katagiri Roshi.
I remember early in the morning, the early sits like we do here, although I think it was another step earlier, maybe the first sit was five instead of 5:30.
I remember him saying something like, "Great autumn moon, high in sky."
Whoa.
We're all half asleep.
And this was at the San Francisco Zen Center place in the city, which they call City Center.
A few of you have been there.
It's the basement of this building, which was originally a Jewish community center actually, with residences, designed by a famous architect, Julia something.
Yeah, thank you.
But anyway, the zendo is in the basement, and there's a bit of a hill, so depending where you are, there are these windows high on the wall.
They must look out onto the sidewalk.
I never went outside and looked in.
So it must be Katagiri Roshi was sitting there facing in, everyone else facing the wall, so you wouldn't really see the window, and looking across.
And it must be that the autumn moon was framed in this little basement window.
It must have been quite a sight.
It inspired him to point it out to us, that we were bathing in the moonlight, whether we knew it or not.
I don't remember what I thought about what I should do with that image, but I remember him saying that.
Full moon, a little hazy in the city sky.
So many of the monks were sitting there, some of them earnestly doing zazen with a lot of effort, some of them snoozing.
They were no different than us.
You know that, right?
They were not better or something.
They were humans.
So maybe he saw this happening and he thought it would be helpful for them to really consider: What are you doing here?
Why are you practicing?
"The world is vast and wide.
Why do you put on the seven-piece robe at the sound of the bell?"
I could ask you the same question.
Why, when [unclear: "Thule"] so generously hit the Han for us, did you come down here?
Why are you following the schedule?
Why are you here at the retreat?
Because the world really is vast and wide.
There's a lot of places we could be.
Or maybe Yun Men was giving a Dharma talk, either opening the talk with this pithy expression, or maybe that was the entire talk.
Back then, the style of Dharma talk was a little different.
It was called Jodo.
What we're doing here is called Teisho.
In Jodo talks, the abbot climbed up on a high platform.
Some places still have this.
I saw it in a Tibetan place once.
I visited the [unclear: "Gomden on Sanlin Island"].
I don't know if this is common, depending on the Tibetan lineage.
There's this little stairs on the side, lots of colors and woodwork.
It probably cost a gazillion dollars to make this thing.
There was a cushion way up there, six, eight feet high, and you'd be sitting or standing down here listening to the teacher.
Probably not looking at him, probably just listening.
The monks would actually stand for the Dharma talk, and the teacher would give it from a high seat.
And they weren't very long, 10 minutes, 20 minutes tops.
There's a collection of Dogen's talks like this in a great book called Dogen's Extensive Record, Eihei Koroku, which means the extensive record by Eihei Dogen.
I say great in a funny way, though.
It's pretty hard to read, actually, because they're very strange and pithy and all coded.
So maybe Yun Men was giving such a short talk, and the monks had to put on their seven-piece robe to come to the Dharma hall and hear the talk.
The bell is rung, actually, before the talk, so that seems likely.
The monks sit in a different place.
They sit in the monks' hall.
That's where the beds are.
They don't really look like beds.
That's where the tatami mats are.
The seven-piece robe refers to this brown robe I'm wearing, which has seven vertical panels sewn together with a frame around it.
The little robes that some people are wearing are a representation of this, except they just have five panels.
And of course, this is religion.
The number matters and the color matters.
There's a lot of information being displayed, if you know how to read it.
A seven-panel robe, they're called seven-joe robe, or when you're hanging out in the Zen sewing shop, they would just say, "Hand me that seven-joe."
"Oh, you're working on a five-joe?
Oh, I see."
A seven-joe is the everyday robe worn for daily practice.
For a big ceremony, you're supposed to wear a nine-joe robe.
I have one of those.
Then, depending on your lofty status and how fancy the thing you're doing is and how fancy the temple is, the number gets higher and higher.
It's the same size thing.
It's really hard to see.
The actual joe is all low contrast, too.
The best signals are subtle, right?
So it's that wide, that's one panel, and then there's a wide overlap in between panels, that big.
But anyway, it goes up to 21 and probably beyond.
In the 21-joe, I've seen one, the panels are obviously a third of these, which is a lot of stitching and piecing when you put it together.
And this outer robe, which goes over one shoulder, is the same kind of robe that all Buddhist clergy wear.
So it's really universal across Buddhism and probably across other religions.
Bob Rose, who's been working on a project in Hawaii, had some local religious leaders, Hawaiian religious leaders, come to a ceremony, and they had a similar thing, a kind of robe over one shoulder.
It looked a lot like Maasai robes, actually.
They wear this robe over one shoulder.
I forget what that's called.
That's kind of all they wear: a little bit of underwear and this red robe over one shoulder, the Maasai.
I was visiting a Maasai village once, and I had on a moonstone fleece jacket.
One of the Maasai guys really wanted to try on my jacket.
It was really hard to get it back.
I think it's not very warm in the evening.
I can't remember the names of things today.
But anyway, the way it's presented has evolved, but all Buddhist clergy wear this kind of robe.
The Dalai Lama does.
The monks of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma all do.
Different colors, some differences in the construction, but basically the same idea, which comes straight from the Buddha.
The story goes that one day the Buddha was walking up a little hill with Ananda, his assistant, also his cousin.
And he said to Ananda, "Look down there, look at the rice fields.
Let's make our robes just like that."
So this overlapping seam is like the path on the rice field, and then that's the rice paddy, which is a wonderful story.
The problem is I don't think it was actually a rice-growing region, so it's probably an Asian story, but that's okay.
That's okay.
It's interesting in traditions like this, the way literal history and religious devotion play with each other.
If we're too literal, it would get pretty boring.
But if we're too religious, it gets really goofy, believing all kinds of crazy stuff.
But it's wonderful.

And he also said to Ananda, "Let's make our robes out of scraps of fabric that nobody wants, scraps from the trash, or even better, scraps from the cemetery, from the charnel ground, where bodies are laid out for cremation, any scraps of fabric that are left or fall off.
That would be the best.
And we'll dye them, so it's all the same kind of drab color."
So this was not flashy clothing.

This was a practice of renunciation for the monks, to wear these very plain robes made from scraps, and also to shave their heads and beards, because the fashion at the time was to wear really bright, colorful clothes and have lots of hair.
Men and women had long hair.
Men had very elaborate beards with little braids in them.
So this is all about letting go, renouncing adornment, renouncing being fancy, being as ordinary as we can.
That's the spirit, but of course things change over time.
And now, unfortunately, having a shaved head is kind of cool.
Oh well.
At least it's the custom.
I don't keep up very well, so I look frumpy.
You're supposed to beautifully shave your head perfectly every five days.
But the spirit is renunciation: to be plain, to be simple, to let go.
One of our practices, which is wonderful, is to sew all the religious clothing by hand, even stitching by hand.
It's a practice of its own.
The idea is that every stitch is like a little prayer, a little mantra.
We say a little mantra to ourselves: I take refuge in Buddha.
I take refuge in Buddha as we make every stitch.
The smaller one and this bigger one.
And there's also color coding, as I mentioned.
When you first ordain as a priest, you make a black one.
Kate and Euan here have sewn, or are sewing, quickly, a black version.
Later on when you finish your training, you receive a brown one.
And one of the great conceits of this is that you make it yourself, but it's not yours.
It only becomes yours when your teacher gives it to you, even though you're the one that made it.
So you don't wear it until you receive it.
It's kind of great, in a wacky kind of way.
Of course we buy nice fabric at the fabric store instead of going to, we should all go to Ragfinery at least.
That would be better.
And Zen sewing geeks are constantly talking about fabric.
It's all they talk about, especially their favorite fabric stores.
Get Chris Brookhart started about fabric stores.
You'll hear a lot.
So maybe in a way we get a step removed in the physical details from the original form, right?
But hopefully we retain something of the essence and the spirit.
This is another step apparently removed in Japan, where most Japanese monks buy their robes.
It's called okesa.
They buy their okesa at a particular store in Kyoto called Matsumoto-ya, which is the trendsetter for Zen fashion.
You have to get your stuff there in Kyoto.
And they're really expensive, so probably your relatives chip in and buy your robe for you.
But regardless of the physical details, the two powerful symbols of our practice are the robe and the bowl.
In Soto Zen we particularly revere the robe.
And obviously we're kind of into the bowls too, you've noticed that.
Thus the hand sewing.
The robe itself is the magical thing, the magical expression of Buddha.
And in a way the only real purpose of a Zen priest is to be a body that wears the robe, that wears the okesa.
So it's the okesa that has the superpowers.
It's the okesa that operates in the middle of the room doing this ritual stuff.
I don't know if you even noticed this, but since the Zen have been closed we had to do a little ritual involving the okesa to begin meditation at 9:20.
So I was in my room working on my talk.
Tuli hit the han, so I had to come down here because I'm the only locally available okesa wearer, so that Tuli could ring the bell in harmony, in sync with the okesa.
That's the only way you could sit zazen.
And then I left again.
So this stuff isn't terribly practical, right?
I know that Tuli knows how to ring a bell three times.
He's very good at it.
But in this case we needed the okesa, so I had to show up.
It all seems like a very big deal.
Here I am wearing the special stuff, saying the special words.
We could do it other ways.
We could take turns giving the talk, for sure.
I know you could all give good talks.
You could take turns sitting in the little copier room talking to each other.
We all know how to talk to each other.
But we don't do it that way, because we're honoring a certain kind of archetypal and symbolic reality that helps us feel a bigger vision in this vast wide world.
Another side, and I hope this isn't too much of a history lecture on Buddhism, but it's good to have some context sometimes.
The Japanese Zen ordination and priesthood is a little different from all the other Buddhist orders.
The more usual plan is that when you ordain to become a monk, you really become a monk.

Just like the Catholic monastics, you give up your birth family, you let go of all your possessions, you live in monastic housing, in a monastery or convent, with basically just your bowl and your robes and your toothbrush, maybe a few books, very few possessions.
You live according to a rule in poverty, in deliberate poverty.
And you change your name.
We receive Dharma names, and we throw them up there once in a while, but you would legally change your name and only go by your Dharma name from then on.
Probably people you meet wouldn't even know your birth name anymore.
So it's a bigger change.
That's usual in all monasticism, and usual in Buddhism.
But in Japanese Zen, it shifted in the 19th century, or the end of the 18th, no, early in the 19th, and mostly for political reasons, actually, historical, political reasons that I will spare you.

The monasticism switched to a lighter, more flexible, from a certain standpoint maybe less real basis, where the ordained people don't really leave their families, and in Japan they do change their names.
We've let go of even that.
Most of us, some people change their names.
My Buddhist name is Nōmon, but you call me Tim, which is fine with me.
Ordaining is still a big deal in our lineage.
Big public ceremony.
It changes your status, and you become a public example of how a committed Zen person is living and being.
It does change your lifestyle, in that you make formal practice a much higher priority.
Coming to things like sesshin and weekly zazen switches from "I'll come if I can" to "I'll be there," period.
But we still keep our basically lay lives.
We still have families, we handle money, we have to get jobs, operating in the world like everybody else.
We can wear religious clothing in everyday life.
Sometimes I wear the kind of Samoan stuff.
But we can also just wear ordinary lay clothing.
Whereas the fully monastic orders wear their robes 24-7, all the time, so they're always recognizably monks and nuns.
There are downsides to this.
It has this quality of partialness, right?
Are you really committing to this thing?
But it has some upsides too.
In this system we're a lot more flexible and we hold the whole thing a lot more lightly.
We know that we're not a big deal.
In certain ways we're not even doing it right, you know what I mean?
So how could we make a big deal about ourselves?
But the beautiful thing is the flexibility, that way we can serve in more flexible ways.
In situations where it would be confusing to have somebody wearing Buddhist religious clothing, we wear regular clothing.
We go to universities and hospitals and jails and streets to help people.
School classrooms.
We don't like to freak people out.

Another advantage is, even in the formal Zen setting, we can remind ourselves and remind each other that there is an appearance of hierarchy and difference, for sure, but that believing too strongly in that hierarchy and difference is really toxic.
It creates a lot of trouble.
We're all just people here.
We're all just bodies, wearing different clothing, for sure, but just bodies.
I think it would be great if there was a really innovative Zen teacher who did naked practice.
We'd have other things to work on, I guess.
We wouldn't have the sense of religious hierarchy.
And I think our system of ordination, when we think about this, is more obviously congruent with emptiness, with the teachings on emptiness.
That yes, I, this person, who seems to have grown from a baby, whose parents named him Tim in 1966, now has a special brown robe and all the special stuff sitting up here.
But still just a person.
Just a person.
And it's just cloth, kind of ratty, getting a little ratty, too, this cloth.
I mean, that's more than you really need to know about Zen clergy, but we're going to keep adding to our ranks, it seems, so it's good to remind ourselves what this is, to reduce confusion somewhat.
But I also think we did receive this system with apparently stages and levels and different statuses.
So let's use it for the good.
And that good can even include confusion about it, right?
Projection about it.
Thinking that the ordained teachers are somehow better than us can be useful.
It can help us see how conditioned we are to want to put ourselves in a certain position relative to other people.
Ultimately in our practice, there is no superior and no inferior, you know?
And also no equal.
No equal.
So think about that.
That's the traditional way of looking at it.
There's no above, there's no below, there's no the same.
It's all empty.
All comparison is empty.
So back to Yunmen's question.
That's why he said it that way.
He was thinking about ordinary monks putting on their seven-panel robe to go to the meditation hall, to the Dharma hall, to practice.
When the bell rings for practice, why do you go?
Why do you go?
Why do you do this practice?
Well, Dogen already told us that there are as many minds as there are persons, and yet they all negotiate their way solely in zazen.
He's a big zazen fan, as you noticed.
Since we all are different people with different minds, we probably all have different reasons.
But here we are.
And why is not a question we usually spend that much time on, right?
Just do it.
That was Katagiri Roshi's other great expression.
Just do it.
Just practice.
Just do it.
Way before Nike.
And zazen, like we're doing these days, held in the container of sesshin, is really pretty powerful practice.
And it's wonderful that we've all been so committed to it.
Not just showing up to sit, but all the forms that weave together to create this opportunity.
Not talking, not looking around too much, just being in our practice.
Every one of us realizing in our own way every moment.
Every moment is so profound.
Every moment is so deep, so rich, so unique.
And the zazen is always happening.
It's not just when we're sitting here.
Waiting for the next step in the meal is zazen.
Eating is zazen, too.
Walking on the grounds is zazen.
Waiting for the tractor to load the wheelbarrow is zazen.
Me trying to load the wheelbarrow just right is zazen.
I mostly had fun, but sometimes John would look at me funny, and I'd have to really concentrate: what am I doing wrong?
Sometimes he'd tell me what I was doing wrong.
Mostly I had the bucket at the wrong angle.
You can't see what angle the bucket's at.
You just have to get a feeling for it, when you're driving tractors.
But by the end of the second day, I received praise.
That felt very good.
"You're a natural on that thing," I think he said.
And receiving praise and feeling my ego inflate a little bit, also zazen.
Painting the cracks on the cabin, turning tan into tan, this is zazen.
So I hope I didn't seem to be knocking enlightenment yesterday.
It's a big straw man, so it's easy to knock it down.
But it's also a beautiful, beautiful and important thing, enlightenment.
And there really are a lot of different experiences that happen in the course of practice that are not like the usual everyday experiences that we think about in our busy lives.
All their normal human experiences, we just don't notice them.
Practice helps us to see a broader range of conscious possibilities.
Some experiences are really subtle, and some are quite dramatic.
And I think more or less they just happen naturally when we're a little more focused, a little more concentrated.
Like I was saying yesterday, some personalities or histories may be more or less prone to these experiences.
And not like one experience is better than the other.
They're just experiences.
You practice equanimity with all these experiences.
But they are notable and important, nonetheless.
And so we should for sure, by all, all by now, be feeling some effects from sesshin.
Otherwise we have trouble answering Yunmen's question.
"I'm just here to hang around with my friends."
Maybe there has been a little more of a feeling of groundedness and openness.
Maybe the occasional moment where everything stops.
You take in something more fully: a sunset, a flower, another human being, a breath.
And some of you I know have had some interesting experiences during zazen meditation.
Everything stopping, sense of stillness, sense of everything just being so far away, so peaceful.
And we could, all of us, be having all kinds of experiences that our conscious mind isn't even aware of.
So don't feel bad if you're like, wait a minute, what about me?
Remember, Dogen said that very explicitly.
You may be enlightened, but not even know it.
Probably we don't know it.
These kinds of particular experiences I'm talking about all seem to stem from some level of concentration.
Concentration is the ability, and all these are natural abilities, right?
We just cultivate them.
But the ability to hold the mind steady, usually on an object.
So we often start with the breath in the body.
Start and maybe finish.
Many, many decades and lifetimes we could focus, concentrate with the breath in the body as the central object.
But concentration is also free of needing an object.
It's a stability of mind.
The object could be not any particular object, but just the rising and passing away of objects in the mind as they come and go.
And the concentration is a stability, a holding, a knowing of what's happening.
There are lots of supporting factors.
Mindfulness is actually remembering that this is our intention, different kinds of focus, and there's this whole complicated system in Buddhism describing how consciousness works.
I think it's really worth thinking a little about concentration without getting too worried about, am I good at it or not?
That's the problem with talking about this stuff.
Right away, half of us are like, oh shit, now I find out how bad I am.
Bad concentration.
The reason we think that is because we think that everything should have a fixed outcome, because we don't yet really believe in emptiness, in which everything is flow and process.
So everything is just flow and process, and concentration as a mental factor is a way to just orient ourselves a little bit.
It's supported by our conscious intention.
I intend to be present these three days, right?
Sometimes people don't have that intention, like, oh, I've got some problems I'm going to think about.
I'll probably figure them out at sesshin, which would be okay.
I'm not so great for this kind of concentration though.
But maybe you'll have a great answer to your problem.
That would be fine with us, right?
Wouldn't that be good?
Ever walked out of here with, oh, excellent, I have a solution to my problem now?
Yeah, and then the poor people who believe too much in this Zen stuff are like, oh, I have no solution.
But I can breathe.
It's nice to breathe.
They'll be unprepared for the problems, but they can breathe.
Who knows which one will work out better though, right?
We don't know.
Concentration features in one of the famous Buddhist lists.
I think we have been bereft of lists, so we need at least one, or we wouldn't be complete.
Concentration is on the list of five powers.
These are the five powers of practice: faith or conviction, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom or discernment.
You don't have to memorize these.
They're in Wikipedia.
Faith or trust or conviction, since faith is a trigger word for some people.
This is translating words in Sanskrit and Pali, right?
Making an English approximation to an idea in another system.
So faith or trust is the first one.
Really, to have some trust: this thing is good for something, apparently.
It must be part of me that was responding to something deep and wise when I signed up for this or got in the habit of doing this for 30 years.
I may not really be able to consciously say when I go home what I got out of it, but I have faith.
I have trust.
I have conviction.
That practice helps.
And this helps to soften up doubt.
Each of these has a traditional opposite, so the opposite of the first power is doubt.
With more trust, doubt has less gravity in our lives.
But it doesn't go away exactly.
We just look at it differently.
The second one is energy.
Norman usually translates this factor, its virya, as enthusiastic energy.
So we're fired up.
When Thule starts the Han, we're not just, oh man, right?
Okay.
We're like, yes!
How wonderful.
Oh, we are blessed.
Which we are.
To have conditions this good for practice?
We're blessed.
We get enthusiastic.
We still follow the form.
Our enthusiasm is pretty subtle, in the Zen style.
I understand enthusiasm, but we express it by showing up.
Sitting in our seat.
Because we know that our sitting in our seat is not just for us, right?
It's for everyone else here.
And it's for all beings beyond that too.

So we're enthusiastic with our energy because we know, wow, not only do I get the great benefits of practice, which I don't know what they are, but I know they're great because I have faith, but I get to help other people receive those benefits.
And so energy works with laziness.
If we didn't have this faith and energy, we'd have a lot of laziness.
We could be binging on Netflix.
None of these are ever present though, right?
In a conscious way, because everything comes and goes.
So it doesn't mean you don't have enthusiastic energy if you wanted to watch TV last night.
What are we supposed to do for entertainment around here?
Goodness.
Just our minds.
The second one is energy: faith and energy.
The third one is mindfulness.
Like I was saying, in the traditional Buddhist context, mindfulness means remembering our intention.
Well, remembering, okay, right, zazen, my intention is to be aware of the breathing, or my intention is to be open and listening.
Oh, sesshin, right, my intention is to follow the guidelines, do my best.
Mindfulness is great because it allows for the fact that we would need mindfulness if we didn't forget, right?
So mindfulness includes and supports forgetting.
So you forget where you are and start whatever you do, if that's a little bit outside of the sesshin container.
Then mindfulness is great because, oh, right.
We don't need to beat ourselves up.
It's a nice thing.
Mindfulness does not beat ourselves up when you screw upness.
It's bringing to mind, bringing back to mind what our intention was.
Mindfulness works with heedlessness, which is not a usual modern word, so I don't know what a better translation is.
Letting yourself spin off heedlessly.
Spaciness maybe?
Maybe spaciness is better.
Spaciness and distractiveness: mindfulness works with that.
The fourth of the five powers of practice is concentration.
That's where I brought up this list, and I already defined that.
Holding awareness on the object or the objectless nature of reality, holding the awareness there.
It's a translation of the word samadhi, which you may have heard.
And that works with distraction.
There's some overlap between mindfulness and concentration.
The last of the five powers is wisdom or discernment.
Buddhist wisdom is not the wisdom of knowing lots of stuff.
Easily confused with that, right?
Oh, he knows so much, he's so wise, wow!
How does he remember all those books?
Some of us don't have minds that can remember all the stuff in the books.
That's okay.
This is a different kind of wisdom.
This is the wisdom of seeing things more clearly, seeing things a little more the way they are, less distorted by our confusion, our ego, our grasping, our resistance.

That's okay. It's interesting in traditions like this, the way literal history and religious devotion kind of play with each other. If we're too literal, it would get pretty boring.
